page: Vultr vx1-m-2c-16g is a memory-optimized cloud compute instance built on the x86_64 AMD EPYC platform. It provides 2 dedicated vCPUs derived from a single physical core with multithreading enabled, operating at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The processor features 48 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of L3 cache, supporting instruction set extensions including AVX-512, AVX-VNNI, and SHA-NI. The instance is allocated 16.0 GB of system memory, establishing an 8:1 RAM-to-vCPU ratio. Bundled storage is limited to 1 GB of local NVMe SSD, alongside a single complimentary public IPv4 address. There are no hardware accelerators or GPUs configured on this instance.

Benchmark testing illustrates a strong disparity between single-core throughput and multi-threaded scaling. In single-threaded compression benchmarks, the AMD EPYC core achieves top-tier results, reaching 39.39 GB/sec in gzip compression and 17.44 GB/sec in bzip3 decompression, alongside a 3609.27 rating in single-core stress-ng tests. However, overall multi-core computational throughput is constrained by the two-thread limit, as evidenced by bottom-quartile results in multi-core Geekbench (2261.0) and PassMark CPU (4920.93) evaluations. Uncached large-block memory read bandwidth averages 45.11 GB/sec, while write bandwidth reaches 39.66 GB/sec. Redis SET throughput measures 4.06 million operations per second, and static web serving delivers 7.66 GB/sec.

The primary technical tradeoff for the vx1-m-2c-16g is the disproportionate balance between its 16.0 GB memory capacity and its minimal 1 GB local NVMe storage volume, which necessitates external block storage or network file systems for persistent data. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the high memory density per vCPU provides an economical footprint for RAM-dependent workloads that do not demand extensive parallel compute. Appropriate deployment scenarios include in-memory key-value caching, single-threaded batch processing, lightweight memory-bound data transforms, and staging environments for memory-intensive applications.
